sources: University of Kentucky Entomology, House Dust Mites (ENTFACT-646): usually visible only under a microscope; primary food is skin scales shed by people and pets, plus micro molds that grow on them; thousands of mites in a single gram of house dust; an infested mattress can hold millions; most numerous in beds, sofas, chairs and nearby carpet; allergenic proteins especially in their feces; adults live about 1-2 months; females lay about 50 eggs; about one month egg to adult; struggle below 50 percent relative humidity; encase mattresses, box springs and pillows in allergen-impermeable covers; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef646

American Lung Association, Dust Mites: too small to see; feed on dead skin cells; get moisture from the air; do not bite, sting or burrow; allergens come from feces, urine and decaying bodies; most exposure happens during sleep; roughly four in five U.S. homes have dust mite allergens in at least one bed; keep indoor humidity below 50 percent; https://www.lung.org/clean-air/indoor-air/indoor-air-pollutants/dust-mites

University of Maine Cooperative Extension, Dust Mites: eight legs; related to ticks and spiders, not insects; https://extension.umaine.edu/home-and-garden-ipm/fact-sheets/common-name-listing/dust-mites/
Texas A&M Field Guide to Common Texas Insects, House Dust Mite: house dust mites do not bite; https://texasinsects.tamu.edu/house-dust-mite/

beats.say: Number seven. Dust mites. Eight legs, cousins of spiders and ticks, and way too small to see.
They eat the skin flakes you shed. One gram of dust can hold thousands.
A mattress can end up holding millions.
They don't bite. It's their poop that makes you sneeze.
Four in five American homes have their allergens in at least one bed.
Dust mites. C tier. No bites, but real allergies, right where you sleep.
